sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active weather pattern will persist into the end of week as a series of disturbances moves through the area. This, coupled with high astronomical tides, will continue the threat for coastal flooding through the end of the week. Rain, strong winds and high elevation snow will remain present in the forecast.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Thursday night)
paragraphs: Latest radar imagery shows rainfall mainly focused over the Olympic Peninsula and along the east side of the Sound and moving north to northeastward. This is allowing some portions of Thurston, Lewis and Pierce county to see generally dry conditions with only a scattered cell here or there. Radar estimated rainfall rates are mostly around 0.10 in/hr...although isolated spots east of the Sound could see rates increase slightly to 0.25 in/hr while SW aspects of the Olympics could see rates getting up to 0.50 in/hr. With Bellingham and Sea-Tac seeing record highs today /only breaking previous records by a degree though/, it does lend support to warmer air in place, keeping the main concern from this system being rainfall as snow levels remain elevated.

Inherited forecast and headlines look good and remain in line with most recent model output. That said, no evening update is necessary. For additional forecast details, please refer to the Previous Discussion Section below and its highlighted breakdown of each hazard.   18
From Previous Discussion...This section will be organized by hazard through the short term period ending Thursday night.

Coastal Flooding: Another round of high astronomical tides will be arriving on Thursday. Another frontal system will be moving inland concurrently, for widespread coastal flooding impacts in waterfront locations. There is potential for major flooding at Friday Harbor, Westport, and Cherry Point, with moderate flooding possible for the rest of the tide gauge locations. Significant impacts have been reported along the Pacific coast as a result of coastal flooding today so be sure to avoid walking on jetties or the immediate coast. The waves are capable of carrying large rocks and logs onshore. The coastal flood threat will ease slightly on Friday.

Wind: Winds will remain elevated through this evening as the front finally makes its way onshore. While winds will ease in Puget Sound overnight, they will remain gusty along the coast and in through the Northern Inland waters of the Salish Sea. The next round of wind, prompting another round of widespread wind advisories, will arrive ahead of the front late Wednesday night into Thursday. The wind direction will be more southerly as opposed to the east to southeasterly winds experienced today. The winds will remain elevated throughout much of the day on Thursday which could make holiday travel more difficult, particularly in along the I-5 corridor. Allow extra time to arrive at your destination.

Snow: A Winter Storm Watch has been issued for the North Cascades including Washington Pass late Wednesday night into Thursday. As much as 15 inches of snow is possible at the pass level and areas above 5,000 feet.

Rain will continue to move onshore tonight and into the overnight hours as the front moves inland. Some of the bands of rain may be heavy at times. Additional rainfall is expected with the next system arriving Wednesday night into Thursday. There is also a slight chance of thunderstorms in the area on Thursday in the post-frontal airmass.

sections.title: Long term (Friday through Tuesday)
paragraphs: Coastal flooding begins to wane a bit on Friday, but the indication is that low pressure over the weekend could bring the threat back per the extended model guidance. There is a brief precipitation break on Saturday for most of the area but additional systems are forecast Sunday and beyond as low pressure returns offshore. This will keep conditions active into early December.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Showers continue across western WA with troughing over the region. The flow aloft is S to SW. Cigs are VFR and will remain as such through the bulk of the TAF period. Usually lower terminals may drop to MVFR overnight, but the general consensus is on VFR conditions continuing. Surface winds will ease slightly overnight, becoming more southerly into the rest of the day Wednesday. The next front arrives Wednesday night into Thursday. Gusts up to 40-45 kts are expected when that next system arrives through Puget Sound. Slightly higher gusts up to 45-50 kts is likely on the coast Wednesday night into Thursday. Expect periods of rain showers throughout the TAF.

KSEA...VFR cigs continue throughout the TAF period with on and off rain showers expected throughout the evening and overnight period. The next period to watch will be late Wednesday night into Thursday as the next front arrives. The winds in that system will be more southerly but have potential to gust up to 35-40 kts.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system will continue to bring strong winds and elevated seas to area waters, with a Storm Warning remaining in effect over the coastal waters, Gale Warnings over both the West and East Strait of Juan de Fuca and Northern Inland waters, and Small Craft Advisories elsewhere. Wind gusts have been somewhat intermittent, but are expected to continue overnight and into Wednesday morning or most areas at Small Craft to Gale strength. The exception will be the Central Strait, where south to southeast winds will experience a lull overnight.

Another frontal passage Wednesday into Thursday will bring another round of strong winds across the region, with Storm Force winds slated to return across the coastal waters by Wednesday afternoon and a handful of headlines elsewhere across the inland waters through Thursday. This frontal system is expected to bring slightly stronger winds than today. In addition, as this system continues to influence the area, isolated thunderstorms remain possible each afternoon and evening through Thursday, mainly over the coastal waters along the coast.
High pressure is favored to build over the region by Friday, bringing a brief break from winds before additional systems bring widespread elevated winds by next week.

Seas around 15 to 25 feet will remain elevated through midday Wednesday before gradually easing to 10 to 15 feet by Thursday afternoon. Seas will continue to lower, reaching 6 to 9 feet on Saturday and Sunday. Seas are expected to build above 10 feet going into Monday.

paragraphs: Ongoing rain will bring an additional 2 to 5 inches of rainfall to the region, with the highest rainfall totals over the Olympic Mountains. While no widespread river flooding is expected, the Skokomish River is still on track to reach flood stage mid week, topping out into moderate. A river flood watch remains in effect for Mason County from Wednesday morning through Sunday afternoon.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active weather pattern is expected through this week with repeated relatively warm systems bringing rain to the region. The first today into Wednesday morning and a second, more potent atmospheric river Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day, and potentially continuing through Friday. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern this week as strong winds offshore and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding. A brief break likely for Saturday, but active weather returns late weekend into early next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active weather pattern is expected through this week with repeated relatively warm systems bringing rain to the region. The first today into Wednesday morning and a second, more potent atmospheric river Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day, and potentially continuing through Friday. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern this week as strong winds offshore and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding. A brief break likely for Saturday, but active weather returns late weekend into early next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Water vapor satellite imagery this afternoon shows the broad low pressure system spinning west of Vancouver Island lifting northward. The associated cold front is pushing onto the coast with rain beginning to spread inland. The majority of rainfall will be focused along the coast, before heights rapidly rise aloft on Wednesday in the wake of the weakening front, leading to a drying trend through the day although rain showers are most likely to linger through Wednesday along the coast and in southwest Washington. Through Wednesday afternoon, there are 60-90% chances of 0.5 inches of more of rainfall accumulating in the Coast Range/Willapa Hills and to the west, 10-25% through interior southwestern Washington, and 10% or less in interior northwestern Oregon including Portland.

An offshore-oriented pressure gradient of -7 to -10 mb between Troutdale and The Dalles will continue to support gusty east to southeast winds across the region through this evening. The strongest winds are expected along the coast as the front moves onshore this afternoon and evening as southeast winds shift out of the south with gusts up to 30-40 mph. Inland, areas of favored gap easterly flow will also see stronger gusts, especially at the western entrance to the Columbia River Gorge where higher terrain and exposed ridgetops may see peak gusts up to 70-80 mph. Elsewhere across the eastern Portland metro, peak gusts of 30-50 mph are more likely, decreasing farther away from the Gorge.

Another area of low pressure over the Northeast Pacific will bring the next period of active weather from late Wednesday through Thanksgiving Day. There is good consensus that a strong atmospheric river with peak IVT of 750-1000 kg/ms will traverse the region, resulting in significant rainfall accumulations. Minimizing the flood threat, however, will be the relatively shorter duration of heavy rainfall and a sub-optimal orientation for forcing peak rates of orographic ascent. Nonetheless, median 48-hour rainfall amounts from Wednesday afternoon through Friday afternoon are 1-2 inches along the I-5 corridor and 2-3.5 inches along the coast and in areas of terrain. In the reasonable worst case (10% chance of occurrence), locales along the coast and in terrain may see up to 4-5 inches while the I-5 corridor may see as much as 2-3 inches. In the case of these higher end amounts, flooding concerns remain largely limited to nuisance flooding of typical low-lying, urban, or other poor drainage areas. As is typical with warm ARs, snow levels will rise well above the Cascade passes, mitigating any winter travel concerns.

As the AR moves onshore, south-southwest winds over the nearshore waters may support a coastal jet, resulting in along-shore accelerations and higher winds out of the south at beaches and headlands. Chances for peak gusts of 60 mph or higher on Thursday remains 30-60% along much of the coast, highest in Tillamook, Clatsop, and Pacific Counties. Have issued a High Wind Watch for the north Oregon and south Washington coast for Wed evening through Thursday morning. Chances for impactful southerly wind gusts of 45 mph or higher within inland valleys are 10-15% or less.

Will also mention, there is a small chance (10% or less) of an impactful surface low that could bring gusty winds to the area on Friday. A few of the European ensemble members show wind gusts approaching 50-60 mph across the forecast area.

Forecast uncertainty increases into this weekend as the majority of long-range ensemble members continue to favor upper-level ridging and relatively drier conditions over the West Coast by Saturday. Chances for further upper-level troughing and associated rain increase again Sunday into early next week. DH/36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00z Thursday...A frontal boundary is currently progressing through the region with a mix of MVFR/VFR conditions at the coast, and VFR conditions inland. Light rain and showers are expected to increase for terminals along the I-5 corridor the next few hours before activity largely tapers off 06-08z. While there may be an additional burst of showers Wednesday mid-morning, dry conditions likely prevail most hours. Better chances for lingering showers along the coast, especially at KAST, Wednesday. Headed through this evening, CIGs likely lower to 4-7 kft at most terminals with the highest chances (20-40%) for MVFR cigs at coastal terminals.

Winds remain breezy near the Columbia River Gorge at KPDX and KTTD with gusts around 25-30 knots slowly decreasing overnight and Wednesday. Within the Willamette Valley, winds instead remain below ~10-15 kt, increasing slightly out of the south near the frontal passage this evening.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions are expected through the TAF period. East-southeast winds will continue to gust around 20-30 knots before slowly but steadily easing tonight. At least this easterly flow helps to maintain elevated cigs through the first portion of the TAF period with only a 10-15% chance for MVFR conditions. Generally dry weather is be anticipated on Wednesday. -99

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Multiple frontal systems will keep hazardous marine conditions in place for the next several days. Currently a cold front is quickly moving across the waters this afternoon with Gale Force winds likely continuing into the evening and overnight hours - most buoys are currently recording gusts between 30-45 knots. We've also seen a rather robust southwest swell building across the waters in addition to southerly wind-driven seas. These two variables likely continue to combine for wave heights of 19-23 ft with a dominate period of ~14 seconds, peaking this evening, before ever so slowly decreasing Wednesday morning.

The daytime hours Wednesday likely provides a brief lull between weather systems while a west-southwesterly swell moves into the waters supporting Hazardous Seas Warnings for seas of 15-20 ft at 14-16 seconds. However, another more robust frontal system arrives late Wednesday into Thanksgiving Day ushering in an additional round of potentially hazardous winds and elevated seas. Based on the latest model guidance Gale force gusts/sustained winds are almost assured, but storm force winds can't be ruled out. Given the 35-55% probabilities for gusts to exceed 48 knots north of Cape Foulweather, a Storm for Watch as issued for the inner and outer waters north of this point. Once this system passes, confidence is high in a return to somewhat calmer weather to end the week into the weekend. Wave heights likely diminish into the 6-10 ft range by Friday night into Saturday morning. That said, models hint at the return of more active weather the second half of the weekend into early next week. -99/36

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect through the middle of the week as the combination of King Tides, elevated seas, and the arrival of fresh swells likely lead to tidal overflow - impacts are most likely at high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. It's also worth highlighting the moderate to high sneaker wave threat today through Thursday. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.

summary.headline: Strong gusts and heavy rain through Friday
summary.lede: Strong gusts up to 61 mph are likely today into tomorrow for Puget Sound, Vancouver Island, and the WA coast. Heavy rain and multi-day flood risk are expected Wednesday through Friday in Southwest BC, with snow possible at mountain passes today.
